doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Rahsaan Roland Kirk and the jazz peak
title: Cannonball Adderley, Cleanhead, and two bands a night at the Five Spot
summary: He never played with Cannonball but recalls Cleanhead's stories. He describes alternating sets with Sonny Rollins and the two-band format, which faded after the mid-1960s.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: ’45 to ’65, I was really in love with the mid-60s and Cannonball Adderley in particular. I loved the combination of his bebop influence but then what we called “soul jazz” I guess, and him in particular. Did you ever play with him?

No, no. Never ever. “Cleanhead” would always refer to him. “I know that little fat boy.” And he talked about John Coltrane. “That little boy played in my band.” You know. So “Cleanhead” was in, and I was playing with “Cleanhead” when he went to New York and he made a record with Cannonball. I was playing with him as a kid, then. That had to be the late 50s. So yeah. But Cannonball, there was a fad, and that was the period, there’s two particular styles that made the music flourish: the bossa nova and the soul to funk that Cannonball played. “Dat Dere”, “Dis —”, you know all of that stuff. And yeah, the world was like, what was his name the General, Patton said oh he was so fortunate to be Patton. General Patton, he was so fortunate to be alive while the world was aflame with war. So with me, I was so lucky in 1959 and the early 60s that the world was aflame with jazz, because we played, we would go on the road for four, six weeks at a time and the New York bands had two bands. We would alternate with Sonny Rollins, alternate with © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-
different people They’d play an hour, we’d play an hour. This was going, there’d be six sets.

Yeah. the Five Spot — not the Five Spot — yeah maybe it was, there on the corner of Third Avenue and St. Mark’s Place. We’d play. We’d come in, and we’d play the first set. We’d play then Sonny Rollins, he’d come in and burn. We’d come back and we’re gonna burn. It would go on, six nights a week. And you would be booked four weeks, six nights a week. Two major bands. On my break I might go over to the Vanguard. “Miles is over at the Vanguard.” To jump in a cab and go over, it was like that.
It was wonderful. And I could feel it, I remember when it began to wane you know.

Like I said, ’66, ’67, ’68 it started to — you noticed they didn’t have two bands anymore. But that was a carryover from World War II. In World War II people were working night shifts, working around, and they’d have bands — okay the bands — we worked from 10:30 to 4. Bands don’t play at four in the morning anymore. That’s ‘cause during the war that’s the way it was with people’s jobs and things like that. And that’s where the two bands came from, that format. But me myself and people that I’ve talked to, now people have jazz at 7:00. That makes sense. We had to make an adjustment. It makes sense. People get home from work. If you live on Long Island, if you live in the city, they don’t want to wait around until 10:00 to come and go home. Come and have dinner, have jazz, then take your drive home. So there has to be adjustments. The one I’m talking about is informal. There was no formal declaration. I’m just telling you as a working musician how I could see what happened.
